turns.doctor_question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me?
turns.patient_response: I came because I just can’t seem to get things in order anymore. My kitchen table is covered with my husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, notes from the senior center, little lists I’ve started and never finished. I sit down to sort it out, and I don’t even know what to do first. Then somehow the whole day goes by and nothing really gets done.

symptom_reasoning.S005: She describes being unable to prioritize and sort multiple papers and unfinished lists, resulting in failure to organize tasks and activities.

turns.doctor_question: About how long has this trouble organizing and finishing tasks been going on—did it start fairly suddenly, or has it been slowly creeping up over months or years?
turns.patient_response: It wasn’t sudden, exactly. It’s been this bad for about a year and three months, since my husband started needing regular help with his appointments and daily arrangements. That’s when I really started getting overwhelmed by it.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes organizing difficulties that have been significantly troublesome for about one year and three months.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient refers to trouble finishing tasks that has been causing substantial overwhelm over the same period.
symptom_reasoning.S081: The worsening difficulties are temporally linked to the identifiable stressor of her husband requiring regular help with appointments and daily arrangements.

turns.doctor_question: Over this past year or so, have you been feeling persistently sad, down, or have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?
turns.patient_response: I don’t know that I’d say persistently sad, no. I get frustrated and worn out, but I haven’t really noticed losing interest in things in that way.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient states they would not describe themselves as persistently sad.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports they have not noticed losing interest in activities in that way.

turns.doctor_question: Besides trouble organizing tasks, have you noticed other changes in your memory, like forgetting recent conversations, misplacing things more often, or having trouble finding the right words?
turns.patient_response: Yes, mostly misplacing things. I’m forever hunting for something I just had in my hand—my car keys, reading glasses, appointment cards. Sometimes it’s a recipe for church supper or the folder I need to bring to the doctor’s office. It happens all the time, and it gets really frustrating.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports repeatedly misplacing essential daily items such as car keys, reading glasses, appointment cards, recipes, and folders, occurring frequently and causing frustration.

turns.doctor_question: Over this past year, have you found yourself worrying excessively about things—like your husband's health or your responsibilities—more days than not, even when there's no clear reason to worry?
turns.patient_response: I’m not sure I’d call it excessive worrying. I do think about my husband’s health and what I need to get done, of course, but it doesn’t feel like worry for no reason so much as just trying to keep up with everything.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed times when you felt confused about what day, date, or season it was, or gotten lost or confused about where you were, even in familiar places?
turns.patient_response: No, I don’t think so. I know what day it is generally, and I haven’t gotten lost in familiar places. I might forget where I put something, but not where I am.

turns.doctor_question: Since this started, would you say these problems with organizing and misplacing things have been getting steadily worse, or do they seem to stay about the same and just feel worse on days when you're more stressed or tired?
turns.patient_response: I’m not really sure. I haven’t kept track closely enough to say if it’s steadily getting worse. It does feel more noticeable when I’m tired or have a lot going on, but I can’t say for certain beyond that.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any new difficulty with tasks you used to handle easily before all this started—like paying bills, using the stove or microwave, or following a recipe you've made many times?
turns.patient_response: Yes… not so much the stove or a recipe, but keeping track of bigger responsibilities has gotten hard. I had to stop leading a big event at the senior center because I just couldn’t keep all the pieces straight anymore. And my daughter has started checking behind me on bills and appointments, because she doesn’t really trust me to manage it all by myself now.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient reports being unable to keep the components of a large event and ongoing bills and appointments organized.

turns.doctor_question: Since your husband started needing more care, how has your sleep been—are you getting enough rest most nights, or has your sleep been disrupted?
turns.patient_response: I’m not really sure. I know I don’t always feel well rested, but I haven’t been keeping track of my sleep. Some nights are better than others, I suppose.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed that your memory and organizing problems get noticeably better on days when you have help with your husband's care or when you're able to rest, or do they stay about the same no matter how much support or rest you get?
turns.patient_response: I’m not sure I can say. I haven’t really noticed a clear pattern like that. If I get more rest or someone helps, I may feel a little less overwhelmed, but I don’t know that the memory and organizing problems actually go away or get much better.

turns.doctor_question: Does anyone in your family—like a parent or sibling—have a history of Alzheimer's disease or another type of dementia?
turns.patient_response: I’m not really sure. I don’t know of anyone in my immediate family who was clearly diagnosed with Alzheimer’s or dementia, at least not that I was told.

turns.doctor_question: Has there been any stretch of time—like a break when a family member fully took over your husband's care—when your memory and organizing problems noticeably improved or nearly went away?
turns.patient_response: No, I can’t think of a stretch like that. I don’t think anyone has fully taken over his care long enough for me to really compare. There may be times I feel a little less stressed when I get help, but I haven’t noticed the memory or organizing problems nearly going away.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed yourself having trouble finding the right words during conversations, or struggling to follow what someone is saying to you?
turns.patient_response: I don’t think so, not in any clear way. I might lose my train of thought sometimes, but I haven’t really noticed trouble finding words or not understanding what someone is saying to me.

turns.doctor_question: Before your husband needed extra care, would you say you were someone who managed organizing tasks, appointments, and paperwork easily and reliably, or was this kind of thing always a bit of a struggle for you even years ago?
turns.patient_response: It’s hard to say it was ever my strong suit, but it feels much worse now. I came in because I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. My kitchen table is covered with my husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, senior-center notes, and half-finished lists, and I’ll sit there looking at it all, not knowing what to do first. Then somehow the whole day is gone.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient reports that organizing has never been a strong suit and is now substantially worse, with difficulty prioritizing paperwork and tasks such that the day passes without progress.
